virals.name: Danny (Dennis) Citrinowicz ,داني سيترينوفيتش
virals.hook:
China Wants the Strait of Hormuz Open — But It Does Not Want Iran to Surrender

Like many other proposed solutions to the Iranian crisis, the idea that China could pressure Tehran into submission is unlikely to work. It reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of Beijing’s strategic interests.

China has a profound interest in the survival of the Iranian regime. In its global competition with the United States, the last thing Beijing wants is a pro-American government in Tehran. Iran remains an important geopolitical asset, helping constrain American influence in the Middle East.

This does not mean China will fight to defend the Islamic Republic. It won't. But Beijing is likely to use its economic, diplomatic, and political influence behind the scenes to help the regime survive, provided doing so does not jeopardize its own vital interests.

Of course, China wants the Strait of Hormuz reopened, energy exports restored, and oil prices brought back down. Its economic interests are substantial, and its relationships with Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and other Gulf states are arguably more important economically than its relationship with Iran.

But here is the critical distinction: China wants stability in the Gulf, not an American strategic victory over Iran.

Beijing may pressure Tehran to reopen Hormuz, reduce regional attacks, or accept a limited diplomatic arrangement. But pressuring Iran to compromise is fundamentally different from helping Washington force the Islamic Republic into submission.

China has considerable leverage over Tehran through oil purchases, trade, technology, and diplomatic support. Yet that leverage has limits. Iran's leadership has repeatedly demonstrated its willingness to absorb enormous economic costs rather than abandon what it considers its fundamental security and ideological interests.

There is another important dimension to this debate. As the United States considers reducing its military footprint in the Middle East, China faces an interesting strategic dilemma. It enjoys strong economic relationships across the Gulf while maintaining close ties with Tehran. A reduced American presence could create opportunities for Beijing to expand its regional influence.

But is China actually prepared to assume greater responsibility for Gulf security? For decades, Beijing has benefited from the American security umbrella without bearing the costs of maintaining it. Protecting shipping lanes, providing security guarantees, and managing regional conflicts would require a fundamental departure from China's traditional approach of limited political and military involvement.

There is little reason to assume Beijing is eager to replace Washington as the Gulf's principal security guarantor.

It is also important to distinguish between China's commitment to the Islamic Republic and its broader strategic interests. Beijing is not ideologically committed to Iran's current leadership. It could accommodate a different Iranian government, provided that government remained strategically independent of Washington. What China strongly opposes is the emergence of an Iran firmly aligned with the United States.

And this brings us to the central problem with the American approach. The Trump administration appears increasingly eager to find a way out of a war that has become politically and economically costly. Turning to China may reflect a recognition that American military and economic pressure alone has failed to produce Iranian capitulation.

But expecting Beijing to deliver what Washington has been unable to achieve would be another serious miscalculation. China may be part of the solution to the Hormuz crisis. It is unlikely to be part of an American strategy to force Iran's surrender.

Beijing wants the war to end, energy markets to stabilize, and regional trade to recover. But it has no strategic interest in helping Washington emerge from this conflict with a decisive victory that strengthens American influence at China's expense.

The bottom line is clear. China wants Hormuz open, but it does not want Iran defeated. And if Washington believes Beijing will force Tehran to accept terms that American military and economic pressure could not achieve, it is likely to be disappointed.

The Iran Watcher
virals.hook:
The Islamic Republic has expanded its war in Europe, using cyber-terror to sabotage France’s food and medical supply chains.

France has formally attributed the sabotage to Shahid Kaveh, a cyber-offensive unit operating under the IRGC’s Electronic and Cyber Center, after the Islamic Republic explicitly threatened Europe with missile strikes and attacks on its “material and non-material assets” in recent weeks.

This was not data theft, propaganda or ordinary cybercrime. The objective was to manipulate physical machinery and inflict real-world damage on civilian infrastructure.

Overnight on October 11–12, IRGC-linked hackers compromised refrigeration controllers across approximately 700 commercial sites in France, including supermarkets, butcher shops, a slaughterhouse and food-processing facilities.

The attackers remotely forced refrigeration units into prolonged, high-temperature defrost cycles while interfering with safety systems.

Food spoiled across major supermarket chains. Equipment overheated. At least 15 fires broke out. French authorities estimate the losses at tens of millions of euros.

The campaign then moved closer to medical infrastructure.

Refrigeration equipment at three French blood-plasma storage sites was targeted in an attempt to raise temperatures and defrost thresholds. Staff detected the attack and moved the products before they were destroyed, preventing damage to the blood supply.

But the intent was clear.

Blood, plasma, vaccines, insulin and other temperature-sensitive medical products can become unusable when refrigeration fails. Attacking the cold chain can destroy essential supplies without placing a single conventional weapon on European soil.

France described the supermarket operation as the first cyber-offensive campaign conducted purely for large-scale physical sabotage on French territory.

Its investigators linked the operation to the IRGC through attack infrastructure, operational tools, Persian-language traces and propaganda channels connected to Shahid Kaveh.

France has summoned the Islamic Republic’s ambassador, opened a judicial investigation, requested international arrest warrants and announced plans to seek further European sanctions.

The attack also gives new weight to the Islamic Republic’s escalating threats against Europe.

On October 31, Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei ordered an “immediate and effective response without geographical limitation” to any threat and called for the regime’s target bank to be expanded.

The IRGC then pledged to confront the United States, Israel and their “regional and trans-regional accomplices” anywhere in the world.

The threats quickly became explicit:

▪️ National Security Committee member Ahmad Bakhshayesh Ardestani warned that if the United States used bases in Germany or Italy, “Iran’s missiles will be fired towards Europe.”

▪️ Former foreign minister Manouchehr Mottaki declared that the next conflict “will reach Europe,” naming Britain, Germany, Italy and Portugal.

▪️ Parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf promised to destroy the “material and non-material assets” of Iran’s enemies without geographical limits.

▪️ Army officials warned that American installations, personnel and interests would become targets wherever they could be reached.

State propaganda reinforced the message.

Hamshahri published a map identifying approximately 15 American and NATO facilities across Europe as potential targets, including bases in Britain, Germany, Italy, France, Romania, Greece and Portugal.

Kayhan warned that NATO facilities “in the heart of Europe” could be attacked. An IRGC-linked propaganda video depicted simulated strikes against European bases and threatened anyone helping the United States.

These were not scattered comments from irrelevant extremists. The Supreme Leader, IRGC, parliament, military officials and state media all repeated the same doctrine: Europe had entered the regime’s expanded battlefield.

The refrigeration sabotage shows what “material and non-material assets” can mean in practice.

The Islamic Republic may lack the conventional capacity to wage war across Europe, but cyber units allow it to strike civilian systems cheaply, remotely and with physical consequences.

Poorly secured refrigeration controllers, water systems, energy networks and other connected industrial equipment become instruments of asymmetric warfare.

The targets are not abstract.

They are the food people eat, the blood hospitals store and the systems ordinary civilians depend on.

The historical irony is difficult to ignore.

France allowed Ruhollah Khomeini to settle outside Paris in 1978. From Neauphle-le-Château, he used interviews, telephone calls and recorded messages to direct the revolutionary movement that established the Islamic Republic.

French territory gave Khomeini the freedom and global media access that transformed him from an exiled cleric into the leader of a revolution.

Nearly five decades later, the IRGC created by his regime is being formally blamed for sabotaging French civilian infrastructure, destroying food and attempting to compromise blood-storage systems.

France once gave Khomeini the platform from which he built the Islamic Republic. The Islamic Republic has answered by bringing its campaign of sabotage onto French soil.

virals.hook:
Here’s where I’d respectfully push back on the logic in this question from @Douthat60 to @POTUS on Iran and Israel:

“Do you have regrets about the decision to help the Israelis do decapitation strikes on Iran? Because that changed the Iranian regime, and it seems like it made them escalate. You could have just kept hitting the nuclear facilities right?” (12:20-12:34)

Wrong. 

- Between the end of the protests in January and the start of the war in February, multiple Iranian leaders said that in response to any attack, no matter how limited or localized, they would go big. And we saw the Islamic Republic do exactly that during the course of the 40-Day War and after.

- As a matter of fact, the Islamic Republic used the period between the 12-Day War and 40-Day War much better than America and Israel did. It revised battle plans and created backstops in its chain of command reportedly 4-levels deep so that it could continue firing during the course of another war. And it acted precisely according to this plan and internationalized the war to distribute pain allowing it to survive decapitation.

- To assume that a more hardline or radical Iranian leadership (presumably under Khamenei Jr) would be able to oversee this drastic shift in Iranian policy and warfighting approach while suffering from the shocks of decapitation and another preemptive attack (2x in 9 months) misreads and minimizes all the planning and state resources the regime (under Khamenei Sr.) put into the interwar period so as to devalue the concept and theory of “limited war” against it so that what Ross offers here could not happen again and again as a cost-free alternative.

- Accordingly, the gains from counterproliferation strikes in the last needed to be better nested into a larger strategy against the adversary while making sense of how it has responded or adapted in order to survive and defend what it holds dear. 

- In my view, the flaw in the administration’s thinking was that Iran was going to be like Venezuela. That is a recency bias. But the larger flaw and mistake folks in the media and analytical / policy community have made since was to think that limited war was a forever option on the table against Tehran. This may be better medicine for proponents of limited intervention, but it was the successes of the 12-Day War that helped the Islamic Republic prepare for and exploit this era, not the failures of the 40-Day War.

outsiders.hook:
China Wants the Strait of Hormuz Open — But It Does Not Want Iran to Surrender

Like many other proposed solutions to the Iranian crisis, the idea that China could pressure Tehran into submission is unlikely to work. It reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of Beijing’s strategic interests.

China has a profound interest in the survival of the Iranian regime. In its global competition with the United States, the last thing Beijing wants is a pro-American government in Tehran. Iran remains an important geopolitical asset, helping constrain American influence in the Middle East.

This does not mean China will fight to defend the Islamic Republic. It won't. But Beijing is likely to use its economic, diplomatic, and political influence behind the scenes to help the regime survive, provided doing so does not jeopardize its own vital interests.

Of course, China wants the Strait of Hormuz reopened, energy exports restored, and oil prices brought back down. Its economic interests are substantial, and its relationships with Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and other Gulf states are arguably more important economically than its relationship with Iran.

But here is the critical distinction: China wants stability in the Gulf, not an American strategic victory over Iran.

Beijing may pressure Tehran to reopen Hormuz, reduce regional attacks, or accept a limited diplomatic arrangement. But pressuring Iran to compromise is fundamentally different from helping Washington force the Islamic Republic into submission.

China has considerable leverage over Tehran through oil purchases, trade, technology, and diplomatic support. Yet that leverage has limits. Iran's leadership has repeatedly demonstrated its willingness to absorb enormous economic costs rather than abandon what it considers its fundamental security and ideological interests.

There is another important dimension to this debate. As the United States considers reducing its military footprint in the Middle East, China faces an interesting strategic dilemma. It enjoys strong economic relationships across the Gulf while maintaining close ties with Tehran. A reduced American presence could create opportunities for Beijing to expand its regional influence.

But is China actually prepared to assume greater responsibility for Gulf security? For decades, Beijing has benefited from the American security umbrella without bearing the costs of maintaining it. Protecting shipping lanes, providing security guarantees, and managing regional conflicts would require a fundamental departure from China's traditional approach of limited political and military involvement.

There is little reason to assume Beijing is eager to replace Washington as the Gulf's principal security guarantor.

It is also important to distinguish between China's commitment to the Islamic Republic and its broader strategic interests. Beijing is not ideologically committed to Iran's current leadership. It could accommodate a different Iranian government, provided that government remained strategically independent of Washington. What China strongly opposes is the emergence of an Iran firmly aligned with the United States.

And this brings us to the central problem with the American approach. The Trump administration appears increasingly eager to find a way out of a war that has become politically and economically costly. Turning to China may reflect a recognition that American military and economic pressure alone has failed to produce Iranian capitulation.

But expecting Beijing to deliver what Washington has been unable to achieve would be another serious miscalculation. China may be part of the solution to the Hormuz crisis. It is unlikely to be part of an American strategy to force Iran's surrender.

Beijing wants the war to end, energy markets to stabilize, and regional trade to recover. But it has no strategic interest in helping Washington emerge from this conflict with a decisive victory that strengthens American influence at China's expense.

The bottom line is clear. China wants Hormuz open, but it does not want Iran defeated. And if Washington believes Beijing will force Tehran to accept terms that American military and economic pressure could not achieve, it is likely to be disappointed.

outsiders.name: Martin
The Iran Watcher
outsiders.hook:
The Islamic Republic has expanded its war in Europe, using cyber-terror to sabotage France’s food and medical supply chains.

France has formally attributed the sabotage to Shahid Kaveh, a cyber-offensive unit operating under the IRGC’s Electronic and Cyber Center, after the Islamic Republic explicitly threatened Europe with missile strikes and attacks on its “material and non-material assets” in recent weeks.

This was not data theft, propaganda or ordinary cybercrime. The objective was to manipulate physical machinery and inflict real-world damage on civilian infrastructure.

Overnight on October 11–12, IRGC-linked hackers compromised refrigeration controllers across approximately 700 commercial sites in France, including supermarkets, butcher shops, a slaughterhouse and food-processing facilities.

The attackers remotely forced refrigeration units into prolonged, high-temperature defrost cycles while interfering with safety systems.

Food spoiled across major supermarket chains. Equipment overheated. At least 15 fires broke out. French authorities estimate the losses at tens of millions of euros.

The campaign then moved closer to medical infrastructure.

Refrigeration equipment at three French blood-plasma storage sites was targeted in an attempt to raise temperatures and defrost thresholds. Staff detected the attack and moved the products before they were destroyed, preventing damage to the blood supply.

But the intent was clear.

Blood, plasma, vaccines, insulin and other temperature-sensitive medical products can become unusable when refrigeration fails. Attacking the cold chain can destroy essential supplies without placing a single conventional weapon on European soil.

France described the supermarket operation as the first cyber-offensive campaign conducted purely for large-scale physical sabotage on French territory.

Its investigators linked the operation to the IRGC through attack infrastructure, operational tools, Persian-language traces and propaganda channels connected to Shahid Kaveh.

France has summoned the Islamic Republic’s ambassador, opened a judicial investigation, requested international arrest warrants and announced plans to seek further European sanctions.

The attack also gives new weight to the Islamic Republic’s escalating threats against Europe.

On October 31, Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei ordered an “immediate and effective response without geographical limitation” to any threat and called for the regime’s target bank to be expanded.

The IRGC then pledged to confront the United States, Israel and their “regional and trans-regional accomplices” anywhere in the world.

The threats quickly became explicit:

▪️ National Security Committee member Ahmad Bakhshayesh Ardestani warned that if the United States used bases in Germany or Italy, “Iran’s missiles will be fired towards Europe.”

▪️ Former foreign minister Manouchehr Mottaki declared that the next conflict “will reach Europe,” naming Britain, Germany, Italy and Portugal.

▪️ Parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf promised to destroy the “material and non-material assets” of Iran’s enemies without geographical limits.

▪️ Army officials warned that American installations, personnel and interests would become targets wherever they could be reached.

State propaganda reinforced the message.

Hamshahri published a map identifying approximately 15 American and NATO facilities across Europe as potential targets, including bases in Britain, Germany, Italy, France, Romania, Greece and Portugal.

Kayhan warned that NATO facilities “in the heart of Europe” could be attacked. An IRGC-linked propaganda video depicted simulated strikes against European bases and threatened anyone helping the United States.

These were not scattered comments from irrelevant extremists. The Supreme Leader, IRGC, parliament, military officials and state media all repeated the same doctrine: Europe had entered the regime’s expanded battlefield.

The refrigeration sabotage shows what “material and non-material assets” can mean in practice.

The Islamic Republic may lack the conventional capacity to wage war across Europe, but cyber units allow it to strike civilian systems cheaply, remotely and with physical consequences.

Poorly secured refrigeration controllers, water systems, energy networks and other connected industrial equipment become instruments of asymmetric warfare.

The targets are not abstract.

They are the food people eat, the blood hospitals store and the systems ordinary civilians depend on.

The historical irony is difficult to ignore.

France allowed Ruhollah Khomeini to settle outside Paris in 1978. From Neauphle-le-Château, he used interviews, telephone calls and recorded messages to direct the revolutionary movement that established the Islamic Republic.

French territory gave Khomeini the freedom and global media access that transformed him from an exiled cleric into the leader of a revolution.

Nearly five decades later, the IRGC created by his regime is being formally blamed for sabotaging French civilian infrastructure, destroying food and attempting to compromise blood-storage systems.

France once gave Khomeini the platform from which he built the Islamic Republic. The Islamic Republic has answered by bringing its campaign of sabotage onto French soil.

دفتر رسانه‌ای شاهزاده رضا پهلوی اعلام کرد که او در آخرین مرحله از سفر اروپایی خود راهی لهستان می‌شود تا «جایزه سلیمان»، نشان افتخاری انجمن یهودیان اروپا را در شهر کراکوف، به پاس حمایت از جامعه یهودیان دریافت کند.

بر اساس این اطلاعیه که دوشنبه ۱۸ آبان منتشر شده است، شاهزاده رضا پهلوی همچنین با مقام‌ها، نمایندگان پارلمان و رهبران جامعه یهودیان اروپا دیدار خواهد کرد.

در این بیانیه آمده است شاهزاده رضا پهلوی همراه با یاسمین پهلوی، با حضور در اردوگاه آشویتس–برکناو، یاد قربانیان جنایت‌های آلمان نازی را گرامی خواهد داشت.

دفتر رسانه‌ای شاهزاده رضا پهلوی نوشت‌: «این سفر تنها ادای احترام به قربانیان گذشته نیست، هشداری صریح درباره تهدید امروز نیز هست. جمهوری اسلامی یهودستیزی و نابودی اسرائیل را به سیاست رسمی خود تبدیل کرده و از خاک ایران به‌عنوان مرکز فرماندهی عملیات تروریستی در منطقه و جهان استفاده می‌کند.»

دفتر شاهزاده رضا پهلوی همچنین بر ضرورت مقابله اروپا با تهدیدهای جمهوری اسلامی و حمایت از مردم ایران تاکید کرد.

outsiders.hook:
Here’s where I’d respectfully push back on the logic in this question from @Douthat60 to @POTUS on Iran and Israel:

“Do you have regrets about the decision to help the Israelis do decapitation strikes on Iran? Because that changed the Iranian regime, and it seems like it made them escalate. You could have just kept hitting the nuclear facilities right?” (12:20-12:34)

Wrong. 

- Between the end of the protests in January and the start of the war in February, multiple Iranian leaders said that in response to any attack, no matter how limited or localized, they would go big. And we saw the Islamic Republic do exactly that during the course of the 40-Day War and after.

- As a matter of fact, the Islamic Republic used the period between the 12-Day War and 40-Day War much better than America and Israel did.
